title: Growing mashua
subtitle: A vigorous Andean climbing tuber with a peppery, pungent flavour.
excerpt: Mashua is a climbing tuber from the Andes that produces a reliable crop of small, firm tubers in autumn. It is one of the easiest exotic tubers to grow in the UK: vigorous, pest-resistant, and tolerant of UK conditions. The flavour is strong and peppery; cook rather than eat raw.
sourceNotes: Cultivation notes from Plants For A Future database (pfaf.org) and Martin Crawford, Creating a Forest Garden (2010). Pest resistance data from Andean crop research. UK growing experience documented by the Agroforestry Research Trust.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sulphur-containing compound found in brassicas, nasturtiums, and mashua. Glucosinolates give these plants their sharp or pungent flavour and are thought to discourage pests and certain pathogens. Cooking breaks most of them down and softens the pungency.

content.text: Mashua (Tropaeolum tuberosum) is related to nasturtium and shares the family's sharp, peppery character. The tubers contain
that make them pungent when raw but milder when roasted or boiled. It is one of the few exotic tubers that performs well in a UK climate without specialist treatment.

Plant tubers in April to May, 10 cm deep, 30 cm apart. Provide a support for the climbing stems: a trellis, fence, or sturdy frame. The stems can reach 2 to 3 m and need something to grip. In the first season the plant establishes; from the second year yields are higher.

Mashua is vigorous and largely self-managing. It is not bothered by slugs, aphids, or most common vegetable pests. The peppery flavour is thought to deter them. Water in the first few weeks until established; after that it tolerates dry spells better than most tubers.

Harvest after the first frost kills the foliage, from October onwards. Dig carefully as tubers are near the surface. Store in cool, dark conditions. Keep back a few firm tubers for replanting next spring. The flavour mellows significantly after two weeks in cool storage.

attrs.title: Cooking mashua
attrs.body: Roasting is the best method: toss with oil and roast at 200 degrees Celsius for 30 to 35 minutes. The exterior crisps and the interior becomes soft with a sweeter, less pungent flavour. Boiling works but leaves the flavour sharper. Do not eat raw in quantity; the glucosinolates are strong enough to cause digestive discomfort.
